anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The write-ahead logging path becomes the primary bottleneck, throttling commit throughput due to slow log generation, flushing, switching, or archiving.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly : The database engine or its background workers hit kernel-enforced ceilings for handles, shared-memory, threads, AIO contexts, or cgroup quotas, blocking further allocation of critical OS objects.

Composite definition: The database simultaneously suffers from log-path saturation and exhaustion of kernel-level resources, so every commit must fight both slow I/O on the log device and the kernel’s refusal to grant the file handles, shared memory, or threads required to advance the log pipeline.

Combined anomalous phenomena: 1) Commit latency, log-write waits, and log-sync waits rise sharply and unpredictably. 2) Log switches or archive operations intermittently fail with OS-level "too many open files", "cannot create thread", or shared-memory errors, causing long stretches where no new log segment can be created. 3) Background writers, checkpoint workers, or replication archivers disappear or refuse to start, leaving redo files to accumulate and filling the log mount. 4) The engine may enter a partial outage: existing sessions hang in commit, new sessions are rejected due to lack of processes or memory, and alert logs alternate between log-related stalls and OS resource-limit errors, making the root cause appear fragmented.

Causal chain: Heavy transactional throughput drives intense redo generation, which increases the frequency of log buffer flushes, segment switches, and archiver invocations—all of which open files, allocate AIO contexts, and spawn or awaken threads. This burst of kernel requests pushes the host toward its per-process or cgroup limits. Once those limits are hit, the engine cannot create the next log file or start the archiver that would free space, so the log device remains busy and fills up, deepening the original log bottleneck. Conversely, the stalled log subsystem lengthens commit paths and multiplies waiting sessions, inflating the number of active processes and open descriptors, thereby accelerating OS resource depletion. The two root causes thus form a feedback loop that amplifies stalls, propagates errors across components, and can culminate in a full transactional freeze.

entry.official_definition: Terminates any session that has been idle within an open transaction for longer than the specified amount of time.
entry.trigger_condition: A session is idle, waiting for a client query, while an open transaction remains active longer than the configured threshold.
entry.workload_impact: The session is terminated; this prevents long idle transactions from holding locks or preventing vacuum cleanup.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
